patch.objective: Recognize postpartum hemorrhage at 1,000 mL within 24 hours, measure blood loss quantitatively, and assess fundal tone and bladder

sources.note: Relayed from the ADN-RN course's earlier cases (read 2026-11-11, primary PDF), not re-read for this band: the pre-licensure RN course is built toward this test plan.
The objective and secondary objectives are the course's own titles.

Relayed from the NCLEX-RN case postpartum-hemorrhage-atony, not re-read for this band; its note: Relayed from the REQ-233 NCLEX-RN cases (read 2026-11-11, primary PDF), not re-read: Physiological Adaptation includes managing a medical emergency and recognizing changes in vital signs; Reduction of Risk Potential includes monitoring for signs of bleeding.

sources.cite: StatPearls. Postpartum Hemorrhage (point-of-care page 27638; title, authors and update date not shown on the page)
sources.note: Relayed from the NCLEX-RN case postpartum-hemorrhage-atony, not re-read for this band; its note: Read 2026-11-14 (summarizing fetch with quotes): ACOG redefined PPH as cumulative blood loss over 1000 mL, or blood loss with signs and symptoms of hypovolemia, within 24 hours of birth by any route; uterine atony is the most common cause; rapid assessment, bimanual massage with uterotonics and ample IV access; methylergonovine 'is contraindicated in patients with hypertension'; carboprost may cause bronchospasm in asthma; tachycardia and hypotension may be masked in postpartum women, so a large loss can sit behind normal vital signs. Re-read directly 2026-11-16 (summarizing fetch with quotes): the point-of-care page still says of methylergonovine 'It is contraindicated in patients with hypertension' and that 'tachycardia and hypotension may be masked'; the NCBI Bookshelf edition of the same chapter (NBK499988; Wormer, Jamil and Bryant; updated 2024-07-19) says it 'is relatively contraindicated in patients with hypertension' and words the ACOG definition as loss 'with signs and symptoms of hypovolemia within 24 hours of the birth process'.

sources.cite: OpenStax. Maternal-Newborn Nursing (2024), section 21.2 Postpartum Hemorrhage
sources.note: Relayed from the NCLEX-RN case postpartum-hemorrhage-atony, not re-read for this band; its note: Read directly 2026-11-16 (web page, summarizing fetch with quotes): PPH is '1,000 mL of blood loss within 24 hours of birth for both vaginal and cesarean births' (ACOG 2017); atony is the most common cause of early PPH; fundal massage 'until the uterus becomes firm' and help emptying the bladder; 'Oxytocin (Pitocin) is the first-line medication to treat PPH'; methylergonovine 'should also not be given to persons with hypertension or preeclampsia.'

sources.cite: Methylergonovine maleate injection, USP 0.2 mg/mL, prescribing information (American Regent, revised August 2025), as reproduced on Drugs.com
sources.note: Relayed from the NCLEX-RN case postpartum-hemorrhage-atony, not re-read for this band; its note: Read 2026-11-16 (Drugs.com's copy of the FDA label, summarizing fetch with quotes; DailyMed itself was not opened): Contraindications 'Hypertension; toxemia; pregnancy; and hypersensitivity'; 'The most common adverse reaction is hypertension associated in several cases with seizure and/or headache'; cerebrovascular accident among post-marketing reactions; IM dose 0.2 mg, 'May be repeated as required, at intervals of 2 to 4 hours.' ACOG Practice Bulletin 183 itself (Obstet Gynecol 2017;130:e168-e186) could not be read on 2026-11-16: the journal page failed to load and PMC copies answered a browser check; only OPQIC's summary page (the definition) was readable.

sources.cite: University of Iowa Health Care. Post-Partum Hemorrhage Management Plan (Bowdler N; updated 2020-12-16)
sources.note: Relayed from the NCLEX-RN case postpartum-hemorrhage-atony, not re-read for this band; its note: Read 2026-11-14 (summarizing fetch with quotes): oxytocin first line (30 units in 500 mL; 10 units IM if no IV); methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM every 2-4 h, contraindicated with hypertension, preeclampsia or heart disease; carboprost 250 mcg IM every 15-90 min, maximum 2 mg, contraindicated with asthma or cardiac, renal or hepatic disease; misoprostol 400 mcg sublingual or 1000 mcg rectal. One hospital's protocol, not a national guideline.

sources.cite: FIGO, ICM and partners. Joint statement of recommendation for the use of tranexamic acid for the treatment of postpartum haemorrhage (2021), restating the WHO 2017 recommendation
sources.note: Relayed from the NCLEX-RN case postpartum-hemorrhage-atony, not re-read for this band; its note: Read 2026-11-14: tranexamic acid 1 g (100 mg/mL) IV at 1 mL a minute, within 3 hours of birth; a second dose if bleeding continues after 30 minutes or restarts within 24 hours. The WHO 2017 recommendation page itself was opened (title and date) but its PDF was not read.
